title: Processes and signals
summary: A running program is a process: find its PID, see who started it, and stop it the right way.

scheme: └── ps   PID 2350   the command you run
text: A running program is a process. Each one has a number, its PID.
- Every process was started by another one, its parent (PPID).
- Your commands are children of your shell.
- PID 1 starts first at boot: on most Linux systems today, it's systemd.

scheme: it can save its work, close its files
no cleanup: half-written files, lock files
text: kill sends a signal: a short message to a process.
- Plain kill asks politely. Try it first, and wait a few seconds.
- kill -9 can't be refused or cleaned up after: keep it for a process that won't stop.

scheme: $ bg %1                 go on, in the background
text: A command ending with & runs in the background: you get your prompt back at once.
- jobs lists what runs in the background of this shell.
- These jobs belong to your shell: close the terminal and they usually stop too.
Something is slow? Find who uses the processor or the memory.
- ps aux lists every process of every user.
- top (or htop) shows the same list, live. q quits.
- pgrep -a python finds processes by name.
